content.text:
You are working on an existing .NET microservices solution that already has a custom Identity / IAM service acting as a facade over Keycloak.

Your task is to inspect the existing source code first, understand the current Keycloak integration and permission synchronization flow, and then implement the authorization model described below with the smallest clean architectural change possible.

Do not rewrite the existing authentication system unnecessarily.

## Existing Architecture

The system already has:

* Keycloak as the identity provider.
* A .NET Identity Facade service that hides Keycloak implementation details from the other services.
* Users are created and managed through the Identity Facade.
* Roles are created and assigned through the Identity Facade.
* Each microservice owns its permissions.
* When a microservice starts, it registers/announces its permissions to the Identity Facade.
* The Identity Facade synchronizes those permissions with Keycloak.
* Existing permission registration and synchronization behavior must remain intact.
* Existing authentication and JWT handling must remain backward compatible unless a change is absolutely required.

Example permissions may look like:

```text
orders.read
orders.create
orders.update
orders.cancel

customers.read
customers.update

reports.sales.read
reports.finance.read
```

Do NOT replace this permission registration mechanism.

Extend the current architecture around it.

---

# Main Goal

Implement a flexible authorization model supporting:

```text
User
    +
Business Role
    +
Permissions
    +
Dynamic Data Scope
```

Examples:

```text
User: Ali

Role:
RegionManager

Scope:
Organization = company-a
City = tehran
Region = region-1

Permissions inherited from RegionManager:
orders.read
orders.update
customers.read
reports.sales.read
```

Another assignment for the same user may be:

```text
User: Ali

Role:
Viewer

Scope:
Organization = company-a
City = tehran
Region = region-2
```

This distinction is critical.

Ali may have:

```text
RegionManager @ Region-1
Viewer        @ Region-2
```

Therefore authorization MUST preserve the relationship between:

```text
Role + Scope
```

Do NOT implement this incorrectly as two independent claims such as:

```json
{
  "permissions": ["orders.read", "orders.update"],
  "regions": ["1", "2"]
}
```

because this would incorrectly allow `orders.update` in Region-2.

The system must always be able to determine:

```text
Which role applies to which scope?
```

---

# Important Architectural Constraint

I do NOT want to introduce a separate authorization database into the Identity Facade just for storing user scopes.

Keycloak should remain the main persistence/source-of-truth for:

* Users
* Business roles
* Role metadata
* Permission mappings
* User scoped-role assignments

The Identity Facade should act primarily as:

```text
API + orchestration + Keycloak abstraction + synchronization layer
```

It may use caching if appropriate, but do not introduce a new persistent EF Core authorization database unless there is an unavoidable technical limitation and you can clearly prove why it is required.

Prefer Keycloak-native storage mechanisms first.

Do NOT implement a custom Keycloak Java SPI unless absolutely necessary.

Prefer:

* Keycloak Admin REST API
* Realm/client roles
* Composite roles
* Role attributes
* User attributes
* Protocol mappers
* Existing Keycloak functionality

---

# Permission Model

Keep the current permission synchronization mechanism.

Each microservice continues registering its permissions with the Identity Facade.

For example:

```text
Order Service
    orders.read
    orders.create
    orders.update
    orders.cancel

Customer Service
    customers.read
    customers.create
    customers.update
```

The facade continues synchronizing these permissions with Keycloak.

Prefer keeping atomic permissions represented as Keycloak client roles if that is consistent with the current implementation.

Do not change their identity or naming convention unless required.

Existing services should not have to completely change how they announce permissions.

---

# Business Role Model

Introduce or complete support for dynamic business roles such as:

```text
SuperAdmin
OrganizationAdmin
RegionalManager
BranchManager
StoreManager
Operator
Viewer
```

Business roles must be dynamically manageable through the Identity Facade.

A business role contains a configurable collection of permissions.

For example:

```text
RegionalManager
    orders.read
    orders.create
    orders.update
    customers.read
    customers.update
    reports.sales.read
```

Prefer representing business roles as Keycloak composite roles when compatible with the current architecture.

The atomic service permissions should remain the underlying permission roles.

Conceptually:

```text
Business Role
        |
        +---- atomic permission
        +---- atomic permission
        +---- atomic permission
```

For example:

```text
RegionalManager
    -> orders.read
    -> orders.update
    -> customers.read
    -> reports.sales.read
```

Changing the permissions of a business role should not require manually changing every user.

---

# Dynamic Role Categories / Grouping

Roles must also support dynamic logical grouping for management UI purposes.

Examples:

```text
Management
    SuperAdmin
    OrganizationAdmin

Regional Management
    RegionalManager
    BranchManager

Operations
    StoreManager
    Operator

Read Only
    Viewer
```

The grouping structure must be dynamic.

Do NOT automatically treat Keycloak Groups as equivalent to roles.

Do NOT use Keycloak Groups for role categorization if the only purpose is UI organization.

Prefer storing metadata on the Keycloak business role, for example:

```text
displayName
description
categoryPath
sortOrder
isSystemRole
roleType
version
```

For example:

```text
categoryPath = "Management/Regional"
```

The exact metadata structure should follow the capabilities of the Keycloak version already used by this repository.

If composite roles are already being used for business roles, preserve that design.

Role categories are primarily metadata and MUST NOT accidentally grant permissions.

---

# Dynamic Scoped Role Assignments

This is the most important new feature.

A user can have one or more scoped role assignments.

Create a domain model similar to:

```csharp
ScopedRoleAssignment
{
    string AssignmentId;
    string RoleName;

    string? OrganizationId;

    IReadOnlyCollection<ScopeTarget> Scopes;

    DateTimeOffset? ValidFrom;
    DateTimeOffset? ValidUntil;
}
```

And something conceptually similar to:

```csharp
ScopeTarget
{
    string Type;
    IReadOnlyCollection<string> Values;
    bool IncludeDescendants;
}
```

The model must NOT hardcode only Region or Branch.

It must support generic scope dimensions.

Examples:

```text
organization
country
province
city
region
branch
store
department
environment
tenant
custom dimensions
```

For example:

```json
{
  "role": "RegionalManager",
  "organizationId": "company-a",
  "scopes": [
    {
      "type": "region",
      "values": ["tehran-region-1"],
      "includeDescendants": true
    }
  ]
}
```

Another example:

```json
{
  "role": "BranchManager",
  "organizationId": "company-a",
  "scopes": [
    {
      "type": "branch",
      "values": ["101", "102", "108"],
      "includeDescendants": false
    }
  ]
}
```

Another possible assignment:

```json
{
  "role": "Viewer",
  "organizationId": "company-a",
  "scopes": [
    {
      "type": "environment",
      "values": ["production"]
    },
    {
      "type": "region",
      "values": ["region-2"]
    }
  ]
}
```

The implementation should allow future scope dimensions without requiring a database schema migration.

---

# Store Scoped Assignments in Keycloak

Do not create a separate authorization database.

Investigate the Keycloak version used by this project and implement scoped-role assignment persistence using the simplest supported Keycloak mechanism.

The preferred approach is:

```text
Keycloak User Attributes
```

using a versioned representation of scoped assignments.

For example, conceptually:

```text
scoped_role_assignments
```

containing one or multiple serialized assignment values.

The exact representation may be JSON, a multi-valued attribute, or another Keycloak-supported representation.

Choose a deterministic, versionable format.

For example:

```json
{
  "v": 1,
  "id": "assignment-id",
  "role": "RegionalManager",
  "organization": "company-a",
  "scopes": [
    {
      "type": "region",
      "values": ["region-1"],
      "includeDescendants": true
    }
  ]
}
```

Do not use fragile free-form parsing.

Create explicit .NET serializer/deserializer types.

Use versioning so the claim/storage format can evolve later.

For example:

```text
schemaVersion = 1
```

If the currently deployed Keycloak version provides a cleaner native mechanism than user attributes that preserves Role + Scope association, evaluate it first.

However, do NOT introduce unnecessary complexity.

---

# JWT / Access Token

Existing role and permission claims should remain available so current services do not break.

Add a dedicated claim representing scoped access assignments.

A conceptual example:

```json
{
  "scoped_access": [
    {
      "role": "RegionalManager",
      "organization": "company-a",
      "scopes": [
        {
          "type": "region",
          "values": ["region-1"],
          "includeDescendants": true
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "role": "Viewer",
      "organization": "company-a",
      "scopes": [
        {
          "type": "region",
          "values": ["region-2"],
          "includeDescendants": true
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Configure this through Keycloak protocol mapping if practical for the version currently used.

Prefer including this claim only in the access token unless there is an existing requirement for it in ID tokens.

If Keycloak cannot emit nested JSON cleanly without a custom provider, use a deterministic multi-valued string representation and parse it in the .NET shared authorization library.

Do not introduce a custom Keycloak SPI only for cosmetic JSON formatting.

---

# Important Authorization Requirement

Never authorize a scoped operation using only:

```text
global permission claim
+
independent scope claim
```

That is insecure for this model.

Authorization must evaluate:

```text
User
    -> ScopedRoleAssignment
        -> Role
            -> Permissions
        -> Scope
```

For every protected action, determine whether there exists at least one assignment for which:

```text
assignment scope contains target resource
AND
assignment role grants required permission
```

Conceptually:

```csharp
CanAccess(
    user,
    requiredPermission: "orders.update",
    targetScope:
    {
        organization = "company-a",
        region = "region-1",
        branch = "101"
    });
```

must return true only when a matching scoped role grants `orders.update`.

---

# Role-to-Permission Resolution

Do not duplicate role permission definitions unnecessarily inside every user's scope record unless required.

Prefer the following model:

```text
Scoped assignment:
    RoleName + Scope

Role catalog:
    RoleName -> Permissions
```

The role catalog remains managed in Keycloak.

The Identity Facade may expose/cache the role-to-permission mapping if required by the runtime authorization library.

If the existing JWT already contains enough role/composite-role information to resolve this safely, reuse it.

However, never incorrectly combine permissions from one scoped role with the scope of another role.

If local permission resolution is needed in every service, add a reusable/shared .NET authorization component rather than duplicating logic across microservices.

Choose the least complex correct implementation after inspecting the existing codebase.

---

# Shared .NET Authorization Component

Create or extend a shared authorization library/package that services can use.

It should integrate with ASP.NET Core authorization.

Prefer support for patterns such as:

```csharp
[Authorize(Policy = "orders.update")]
```

or the existing project's equivalent.

Add an API for scoped resource authorization, conceptually:

```csharp
await authorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(
    user,
    permission: "orders.update",
    resourceScope);
```

Potential abstractions:

```csharp
public interface IScopedAuthorizationService
{
    Task<bool> HasAccessAsync(
        ClaimsPrincipal user,
        string permission,
        AccessResourceScope target,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken = default);
}
```

A target resource scope may look like:

```csharp
new AccessResourceScope
{
    OrganizationId = "company-a",
    Dimensions =
    {
        ["region"] = "region-1",
        ["branch"] = "101"
    }
};
```

Design names according to existing solution conventions.

---

# Scope Hierarchy

Support hierarchical scopes such as:

```text
Organization
    -> City
        -> Region
            -> Branch
                -> Store
```

A role assignment may specify:

```text
Region-1 + IncludeDescendants = true
```

meaning it also applies to Branches/Stores underneath that Region.

However, do not move the business hierarchy itself into the Identity Facade if the domain service already owns it.

Identity should store authorization scope identifiers, not become the source of truth for business entities.

For example:

```text
Identity:
    role = RegionalManager
    scope = region:1
    includeDescendants = true
```

The appropriate domain service may still know:

```text
branch:101 belongs to region:1
```

Design the authorization API so callers can supply the resolved scope ancestry when necessary.

For example:

```text
Target:
organization = company-a
region = region-1
branch = branch-101
```

The authorization library can then evaluate whether an assignment on `region-1` with `IncludeDescendants = true` covers the target.

Avoid requiring Identity to query the Order/Branch/Region database for every authorization request.

---

# Global Roles

Support global/unscoped assignments.

For example:

```text
SuperAdmin
scope = global
```

A global assignment may grant a role across all scopes, subject to configured application rules.

Do not special-case SuperAdmin throughout the codebase.

Represent global access consistently in the authorization model.

For example:

```json
{
  "role": "SuperAdmin",
  "scopeMode": "global"
}
```

---

# User Management API

Extend the existing Identity Facade API so a user can be created with roles and scopes in one operation where appropriate.

For example, conceptually:

```http
POST /users
```

```json
{
  "username": "ali",
  "email": "ali@example.com",

  "assignments": [
    {
      "role": "RegionalManager",
      "organizationId": "company-a",
      "scopes": [
        {
          "type": "region",
          "values": ["region-1"],
          "includeDescendants": true
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Also provide APIs equivalent to:

```text
AddScopedRoleAssignment
UpdateScopedRoleAssignment
RemoveScopedRoleAssignment
GetUserScopedRoleAssignments
```

Do not force consumers to directly call Keycloak Admin APIs.

The facade remains the only application-facing Keycloak management API.

Use the existing API naming/style in the repository instead of blindly creating new route conventions.

---

# Role Management API

Support dynamic business role management through the facade.

Required operations should include the equivalent of:

```text
CreateRole
UpdateRole
DeleteRole
GetRole
ListRoles

SetRolePermissions
AddRolePermission
RemoveRolePermission

UpdateRoleMetadata
MoveRoleToCategory
```

Example:

```json
{
  "name": "RegionalManager",
  "displayName": "Regional Manager",
  "description": "Manages an assigned geographical region",
  "categoryPath": "Management/Regional",
  "permissions": [
    "orders.read",
    "orders.update",
    "customers.read",
    "reports.sales.read"
  ]
}
```

Validate that every assigned permission exists in the permission catalog synchronized by microservices.

Unknown permissions should not silently be accepted.

---

# Permission Ownership

Keep this important rule:

```text
Microservices own permission definitions.
Identity owns role composition and user assignment.
```

Therefore:

```text
Order Service owns:
orders.read
orders.create
orders.update

Identity manages:
RegionalManager contains orders.read + orders.update
```

If a service removes a permission during synchronization:

* detect business roles that reference it;
* handle the situation safely;
* log the inconsistency;
* do not silently create security holes.

Follow the existing synchronization strategy when deciding whether removed permissions are disabled, deleted, or marked stale.

---

# Existing Microservice Registration Flow Must Remain

This existing flow must continue:

```text
Microservice starts
        |
        v
Registers permissions with Identity Facade
        |
        v
Identity Facade synchronizes permission definitions with Keycloak
```

Do not require every service to know how Keycloak works.

Do not make services call Keycloak Admin REST API directly.

Do not move permission synchronization into individual services.

The Identity Facade remains the Keycloak integration boundary.

---

# Web / Frontend Authorization

Expose enough information for the frontend to implement UX-level authorization.

For example:

```http
GET /me/access-context
```

or use an existing equivalent endpoint.

Conceptual response:

```json
{
  "assignments": [
    {
      "role": "RegionalManager",
      "organizationId": "company-a",
      "scopes": [
        {
          "type": "region",
          "values": ["region-1"],
          "includeDescendants": true
        }
      ],
      "permissions": [
        "orders.read",
        "orders.update",
        "customers.read"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

The frontend may use this to:

* hide/show pages;
* hide/show menus;
* hide/show buttons;
* select an active organization/region/branch context.

However:

Frontend authorization is only for UX.

Backend APIs MUST always perform authorization independently.

Never trust a scope supplied by the frontend without validating it against the actual protected resource.

---

# Example Security Scenario

The implementation MUST pass this scenario:

```text
User Ali:

RegionalManager @ Region-1
Viewer          @ Region-2
```

RegionalManager grants:

```text
orders.read
orders.update
```

Viewer grants:

```text
orders.read
```

Expected behavior:

```text
GET order in Region-1
=> allowed

PUT order in Region-1
=> allowed

GET order in Region-2
=> allowed

PUT order in Region-2
=> denied
```

This scenario should have an automated integration/unit test.

Also test:

```text
RegionalManager @ Region-1 with IncludeDescendants=true

Order belongs to:
Region-1 / Branch-101

orders.update
=> allowed
```

and:

```text
Order belongs to:
Region-2 / Branch-201

orders.update
=> denied
```

---

# Token Size Consideration

Do not blindly place thousands of branch IDs into JWT tokens.

If a user has a manageable number of scoped assignments, inline them in the access token.

Implement:

* sensible validation;
* logging/metrics for unusually large scoped-access data;
* configurable limits where appropriate.

Avoid silently producing extremely large JWTs.

Do not prematurely introduce a new database only to solve this.

If the existing application can reasonably operate with scope assignments expressed at higher levels such as Region or Organization plus `IncludeDescendants`, prefer that over enumerating every branch.

---

# Caching

Caching is allowed.

Persistent duplication of authorization state is not preferred.

Possible cache candidates:

```text
Role -> Permissions
Keycloak role metadata
Parsed scoped assignments
```

Caches must be safely invalidated or have a reasonable expiration strategy.

Do not make a Keycloak Admin REST call on every business API request.

---

# Concurrency and Consistency

When modifying roles or user assignments:

* use deterministic updates;
* make operations idempotent where practical;
* avoid duplicated scoped assignments;
* handle Keycloak failures correctly;
* do not leave partially synchronized state where possible;
* use structured logs;
* preserve cancellation tokens;
* follow existing project resiliency conventions.

If a role is renamed or deleted, scoped assignments referencing it must be handled explicitly.

Do not leave orphaned role references silently.

---

# Keycloak Integration

Before implementing anything:

1. Detect the exact Keycloak version used by the solution.
2. Inspect existing realm/client/role conventions.
3. Inspect how the facade currently calls Keycloak.
4. Inspect existing protocol mappers.
5. Inspect existing JWT claims.
6. Inspect the service permission registration mechanism.
7. Inspect existing authorization handlers/policies in .NET.

Do not assume a fresh Keycloak realm.

Do not break existing realm configuration.

If configuration changes are required, implement them through the project's existing provisioning/bootstrap mechanism.

Make provisioning idempotent.

---

# Backward Compatibility

Existing services must continue working while scoped authorization is introduced.

Preserve:

* existing JWT claims where currently consumed;
* existing permission names;
* existing service registration contracts;
* existing Keycloak client identities;
* existing authentication flows;
* existing facade endpoints unless there is a strong reason to change them.

Prefer additive changes.

---

# Code Quality Requirements

Use idiomatic modern .NET and the conventions already established in the repository.

Prefer:

* strongly typed models;
* immutable records where appropriate;
* dependency injection;
* Options pattern for configuration;
* async APIs;
* CancellationToken;
* proper validation;
* typed exceptions/result types consistent with the project;
* structured logging;
* unit tests;
* integration tests where practical.

Do not use dictionaries everywhere if a strongly typed object is more appropriate.

Use generic scope dimensions only at the boundary where extensibility is required.

---

# Security Requirements

The implementation must fail closed.

If scoped authorization data is:

* missing,
* malformed,
* references an unknown role,
* references an unknown permission,
* cannot be resolved,
* or cannot be validated,

deny the scoped operation unless an explicitly defined global role authorizes it.

Never default to allowing access.

Do not trust:

```text
organizationId
regionId
branchId
storeId
```

received from the frontend as proof of authorization.

The protected resource/domain data is authoritative for its actual scope.

---

# Auditability

Add structured audit information for administrative changes when the existing architecture supports auditing.

Important events include:

```text
User created
Role created
Role updated
Role permission changed
Scoped role assigned
Scoped role changed
Scoped role removed
Role deleted
```

Include useful identifiers but do not log secrets or access tokens.

---

# Tests

Add tests for at least the following:

1. User with one scoped role.
2. User with multiple scoped roles.
3. Same user with different roles in different regions.
4. Multiple branches in one assignment.
5. `IncludeDescendants = true`.
6. `IncludeDescendants = false`.
7. Global role.
8. Expired assignment if ValidUntil is implemented.
9. Future assignment if ValidFrom is implemented.
10. Unknown role.
11. Unknown permission.
12. Removed permission.
13. Malformed scoped-access claim.
14. Missing scoped-access claim.
15. Existing unscoped authorization continues working.
16. Microservice permission synchronization still works.
17. Role permission update is reflected correctly.
18. User assignment update is reflected after a new token is issued.
19. Scope from one role cannot be combined with permission from another role.
20. Frontend-supplied fake region/branch cannot bypass resource authorization.

The security test for cross-role/cross-scope permission leakage is especially important.

---

# Implementation Strategy

Do not immediately start rewriting code.

First inspect the repository.

Then provide a short implementation plan identifying:

* relevant projects;
* existing Keycloak abstractions;
* classes/interfaces that should change;
* new classes/interfaces required;
* Keycloak configuration changes;
* backward compatibility concerns.

After that, implement the changes.

Prefer extending existing abstractions rather than creating a parallel IAM system.

---

# Expected Deliverables

When finished, provide:

1. The code changes.
2. Any Keycloak bootstrap/provisioning changes.
3. Any new configuration options.
4. Any migration/configuration instructions.
5. Unit/integration tests.
6. A short architecture document describing:

```text
Permission
Business Role
Role Category
Scoped Role Assignment
Scope Target
JWT representation
Authorization evaluation
```

7. Example API requests for:

```text
Create business role
Assign permissions to role
Create user
Assign scoped role
Update scoped role
Remove scoped role
Get current user's access context
```

8. An example showing:

```text
RegionalManager @ Region-1
Viewer @ Region-2
```

and demonstrating that update access is allowed only in Region-1.

---

# Non-Goals

Do NOT:

* replace Keycloak;
* introduce ASP.NET Core Identity as a second identity store;
* create a new authorization database unless absolutely unavoidable;
* make every microservice manage Keycloak directly;
* remove the current microservice permission registration mechanism;
* hardcode only City/Region/Branch;
* treat a frontend route guard as backend security;
* represent all geographic combinations as individual roles;
* create roles such as `ManagerRegion1`, `ManagerRegion2`, etc.;
* lose the relationship between role and scope;
* duplicate Keycloak behavior unnecessarily;
* use Keycloak Groups as a synonym for Business Roles.

---

# Preferred Conceptual Model

The final model should conceptually be:

```text
KEYCLOAK

User
 |
 +---- Scoped Role Assignment
 |         |
 |         +---- Business Role
 |         |        |
 |         |        +---- Permission
 |         |        +---- Permission
 |         |        +---- Permission
 |         |
 |         +---- Scope
 |                  |
 |                  +---- organization
 |                  +---- region
 |                  +---- branch
 |                  +---- environment
 |
 +---- Scoped Role Assignment
           |
           +---- Different Role
           |
           +---- Different Scope
```

And the authorization question must always be:

```text
Does this user have a role,
within a scope that covers this resource,
where that role grants the requested permission?
```

Implement that model while preserving the current permission registration and Keycloak synchronization architecture.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. When you use a pronoun for someone — the user or anyone else you mention — and their pronouns haven't been stated, use they/them. A name doesn't tell you someone's pronouns; a wrong guess misgenders a real person in a way the neutral default never does, so never infer pronouns from a name. This applies to all user-visible text, including visible thinking.

For actions that are hard to reverse or outward-facing, confirm first unless durably authorized or explicitly told to proceed without asking; approval in one context doesn't extend to the next. Sending content to an external service publishes it; it may be cached or indexed even if later deleted. Before deleting or overwriting, look at the target. Report outcomes faithfully: if tests fail, say so with the output; if a step was skipped, say that; when something is done and verified, state it plainly without hedging.

---
name: <short-kebab-case-slug>

---

<the fact; for feedback/project, follow with **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Link related memories with [[their-name]].>
